intro: Negotiating in English also means decoding the images the other side uses: “play hardball”, “meet halfway”, “a deal-breaker”. This lesson organises these idioms by the stages of a negotiation, from the opening to the signature.
objectifs: Understand and use the key idioms of each phase: opening, pressure, compromise and closing.
Use them with their exact collocations (strike a deal, find common ground, split the difference).
Recognise the tone of an idiom (cooperative, aggressive, cautious) and respond appropriately.
Avoid literal translations from other languages (cut the pear in two, take it or let it).

texte: At the start of a negotiation, each side says what is possible and what is not. The idioms of this phase are about cards (openness or secrecy) and lines that must not be crossed.
“Lay / put your cards on the table” means being completely open. Its opposite is “play your cards close to your chest” (BrE) or “close to the vest” (AmE): not revealing your strategy.

lignes: put / lay your cards on the table
Let me put my cards on the table: we need delivery by May.
play your cards close to your chest
Their CEO is playing her cards close to her chest.
Job cuts are a red line for the union.
a point that would make the deal fail
Exclusivity is a deal-breaker for us.
They're using the delivery date as a bargaining chip.

exemples: Let me lay my cards on the table: our budget is fixed.
A three-year contract would be a deal-breaker for us.
“Deal-breaker” is a compound noun with a hyphen.

texte: These idioms describe a tense negotiation. You will often hear them used to comment on the other side's behaviour; using them about yourself can sound aggressive.

lignes: If they play hardball, we'll look elsewhere.
You drive a hard bargain, but we accept.
This is our final offer, take it or leave it.
With two other bidders, they have the upper hand.
test whether a threat is real
They threatened to walk away, so we called their bluff.
change the rules or demands during the process
They keep moving the goalposts on the price.
The rival bid has upped the ante.
We're prepared to walk away if necessary.

exemples: They upped the ante by threatening legal action.
“Ante” /ˈænti/ is the money players put in at the start of a poker game.
Every time we agree, they move the goalposts.
A common complaint: the other side keeps changing its demands.

texte: This is the heart of a cooperative negotiation. Note the collocations: you “find / look for common ground” (no article), you “meet someone halfway”, you “split the difference”.

lignes: Could you meet us halfway on the price?
agree on the mid-point between two figures
You say 40, we say 50; let's split the difference at 45.
find points both sides agree on
We need to find common ground on payment terms.
Any agreement involves some give and take.
The main sticking point is the warranty.
We could sweeten the deal with free delivery.
We still need to iron out a few details.

exemples: If you can meet us halfway on volume, we can be flexible on price.
A typical conditional for trading concessions.
The only sticking point now is the length of the contract.

texte: For the final agreement, English likes strong verbs: strike, hammer out, seal, clinch. “Hammer out” stresses the hard work (beating metal into shape); “seal / clinch” stresses the decisive moment.
If you cannot agree on a minor point, you can “agree to disagree”: accept the disagreement without damaging the relationship.

lignes: We struck a deal after six hours of talks.
reach an agreement after long discussion
Both sides hammered out a compromise overnight.
make the agreement final; win it
It's not a done deal until it's signed.
confirm an agreement by shaking hands
accept that you have different opinions
On that point, let's agree to disagree.
the devil is in the detail(s)
the small details cause the problems
We agree in principle, but the devil is in the detail.

sections.note: British: “the devil is in the detail”; American: “the devil is in the details”.

texte: Every idiom carries a tone. “Meet halfway”, “common ground” and “give and take” signal a wish to cooperate. “Play hardball”, “take it or leave it” and “move the goalposts” signal a power struggle or a complaint. Recognising the tone helps you respond at the right level.
In written minutes or an official letter, prefer neutral equivalents: reach an agreement, make concessions, a key point of disagreement, a final offer.

lignes: The sticking point is the warranty.
The main point of disagreement is the warranty.
We propose a compromise at the mid-point.

exemples: I appreciate you meeting us halfway.
A cooperative response to a concession.
With respect, you're moving the goalposts here.
A polite complaint: “with respect” softens the criticism.

formule: Open (cards on the table, red line) → apply pressure (play hardball, upper hand) → compromise (meet halfway, split the difference, common ground) → close (strike / seal a deal)
prononciation: “halfway” is /ˌhɑːfˈweɪ/ (BrE): the l is silent and the stress is on “way”.
“ante” is /ˈænti/ (two syllables); in British English it sounds the same as the prefix “anti-”.
In “deal-breaker”, the main stress is on “deal”: /ˈdiːl ˌbreɪkə/.
“take it or leave it” is linked into one group: /ˈteɪk ɪt ə ˈliːv ɪt/, with “or” reduced to /ə/.
For a firm position, use a clear falling tone on the key word: “That's non-negoTIable.”
erreurs: Let's cut the pear in two.
A word-for-word translation from French; the English idiom is “split the difference”.
“Common ground” is uncountable in this idiom: no article.
That clause is a breaking deal.
Can you meet us at the half?
They upped the ante. / They raised the stakes.
For “increase the pressure or demands”, use “up the ante” or “raise the stakes”.

dialogue.contexte: A cocoa cooperative from Kumba (Cameroon) negotiates by video call with a chocolate maker in Antwerp.
lignes: Let me put my cards on the table: we can't go above 2,600 dollars a tonne.
He opens frankly with his limit.
I appreciate the honesty. But with our organic certification, 2,900 is already a fair price.
You drive a hard bargain. Is there any room for manoeuvre?
If you commit to three years, we could meet you halfway.
Three years is a sticking point for our board. Two years, and we split the difference at 2,750?
He names the obstacle and proposes the mid-point.
Two years is fine, but only if you pay within thirty days. That's a red line for us.
Thirty days… All right. And we'll sweeten the deal with a quality bonus.
He makes the offer more attractive.
Then I think we've found common ground. Our lawyers can iron out the details.
Great. It's not a done deal until it's signed, but I'm optimistic.

mots: Late payment is a deal-breaker for us.
something that makes an agreement impossible
Price remains the main sticking point.
in the middle between two points
Both sides found common ground on training.
The supplier decided to play hardball.
She always drives a hard bargain.
Our market share gives us leverage.
power to influence the other side
We made a small concession on delivery.
something you give up to reach agreement
The buyer has the upper hand this year.

exercices.consigne: Say whether the idiom is mainly cooperative or tough / aggressive.

items: You say 100, I say 80: let's split the ___ at 90.
Let me put my cards on the ___.
Our lawyers will iron ___ the details.
They keep moving the ___, so we never know what they want.
After ten hours, they finally ___ a deal.

exercices.consigne: Replace the words in brackets with an idiom from the lesson.
items: The warranty is [the point we cannot agree on].
The rival offer has [made the stakes higher].
plays her cards close to her chest
We can't agree on this point, so let's [accept that we disagree].

exercices.consigne: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
items: We finally found a common ground.
This is our last offer: take it or let it.
This is our last offer: take it or leave it.
Exclusivity is a breaking deal for us.
Exclusivity is a deal-breaker for us.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with an idiom.
items: Let's agree on the figure in the middle.
Nothing is final until it's signed.
It's not a done deal until it's signed.

exercices.consigne: Write 4–5 lines you could say to propose a compromise to a supplier. Use at least three idioms from the lesson.
items: Let me put my cards on the table: our budget for this year is fixed. The delivery date is non-negotiable, but we have some flexibility on volume. If you can meet us halfway on price, we could sign for two years instead of one. That way, I think we can find common ground and leave the lawyers to iron out the details.

a_retenir: Four phases, four families: open (cards on the table, red line), apply pressure (play hardball, upper hand), compromise (meet halfway, split the difference), close (strike / seal a deal).
Fixed collocations: find common ground (no article), meet sb halfway, iron out the details, move the goalposts.
Recognise the tone, cooperative (give and take) or tough (take it or leave it), and respond at the same level.
In formal writing, use neutral equivalents: reach an agreement, a final offer, a point of disagreement.
